claims.text: The untreated refractory high-entropy alloy forms non-protective, rapidly growing oxide layers under extreme-temperature exposure.
Adding approximately 2–3 at.% Al to a refractory high-entropy alloy will promote formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 scale.
The Al addition will significantly improve oxygen resistance relative to the untreated alloy.
The intervention consists of incorporating a small Al addition during melting or casting.
The proposed effect should occur during exposure at approximately 1200°C in ambient air or a controlled oxygen-rich atmosphere for 100 hours.
A continuous, adherent alumina scale acts as a barrier to oxygen ingress.
At high temperature, added Al preferentially oxidizes to form Al2O3.
The resulting Al2O3 is thermodynamically stable and slow-growing.
The Al2O3 scale reduces oxygen diffusion into the bulk alloy and thereby limits further oxidation.
The Al-modified alloy will have lower oxidation mass gain than the untreated alloy.
The Al-modified alloy will have a thinner and more uniform oxide scale than the untreated alloy.
Insufficient Al content may prevent formation of a continuous alumina layer.
Phase-distribution issues may hinder oxide-scale adherence or integrity.
HEA phase stability and decomposition length scale can depend on composition and annealing temperature.
The optimal Al concentration and its interaction with the existing microstructure require further validation.
Failure to obtain both a statistically significant reduction in mass gain and a continuous, adherent Al2O3 scale under identical conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
